blocks.content: An IP address is good at exactly one job: getting a piece of data to the right device. It gets a packet across the internet, through however many routers stand in the way, and drops it at your laptop, your phone, or a server sitting in a data center somewhere. That part of the journey, the part covered by the Internet layer, ends the moment the data arrives at the correct machine.

But a single device is rarely doing just one thing on the network at once. Right now your laptop might have a browser open with several tabs, an email client quietly checking for new mail, and maybe a game keeping its connection alive in the background. All of them are sending and receiving network data at the same time, over the same one IP address. When a packet lands on that device, something still has to decide which of those programs it actually belongs to.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436868213-428330969.png
1. The Problem Ports Actually Solve

This is the exact gap the Transport layer exists to close, and it is worth sitting with the problem for a moment before jumping to the answer. The Internet layer, which you met in the Networking Fundamentals module, only understands devices. It has no concept of a browser, an email client, or a game. As far as IP is concerned, once a packet reaches the right machine, its job is done.

The operating system on that machine is the one left holding the packet, and it needs a fast, reliable way to hand that packet to the correct running program without guessing. Guessing is not good enough at internet scale, where a single machine can be juggling dozens or hundreds of active connections in any given second. There has to be a number stamped directly onto the data that says, in effect, this piece belongs to that specific program and no other.

blocks.title: Where this sits in the model
blocks.content: This is precisely the job of the Transport layer, the third layer in the four layer TCP/IP model you already covered. The Internet layer gets data to the right device. The Transport layer, starting with the idea you are about to learn here, gets it the rest of the way to the right program on that device.
2. Ports, Defined Precisely

A port is a number, from 0 to 65535, that identifies a specific application or service running on a device. It is not a physical thing, there is no actual socket or slot on your motherboard that corresponds to port 443. It is a purely logical label the operating system uses to keep track of which running program owns which conversation.

Every piece of data crossing the Transport layer is stamped with two of these numbers at once: a source port and a destination port. This ties directly back to the encapsulation topic you already covered. Remember that the Transport layer wraps data into a segment by adding its own header, and the source port and destination port are exactly what live inside that segment header, right alongside the data itself.

Put the two ideas from this module and the last one together and you get a complete, precise picture. The IP address gets data to the right building. The port number gets it to the right room inside that building. Neither one alone is enough, and both numbers travel together on every single segment that crosses the network.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436868213-578882585.png
3. The Three Ranges of Port Numbers
blocks.text: 3. The Three Ranges of Port Numbers

blocks.content: Port numbers are not handed out randomly. They are split into three clearly defined ranges, each with a different purpose and a different level of official control. Knowing these ranges is genuinely useful day to day, because the range a port falls into tells you a lot about what kind of service is probably listening on it.

{"headers":["Range","Numbers","What it is for"],"rows":[["Well known ports","0 to 1023","Reserved for standard, universally recognized services. Requires administrator privileges to bind to on most operating systems."],["Registered ports","1024 to 49151","Registered with an official authority for a specific application, but not as tightly controlled as well known ports."],["Dynamic or ephemeral ports","49152 to 65535","Temporarily assigned by the operating system, usually for the client side of an outgoing connection."]]}

The pattern across all three ranges is really about trust and permanence. Well known ports are the most tightly controlled because everyone on the internet needs to agree on them in advance, otherwise your browser would have no idea which port to try when it wants to reach a web server. Ephemeral ports sit at the opposite end, handed out freely and temporarily, because they only need to mean something for the lifetime of one connection.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436868213-702142392.png
blocks.alt: The Three Ranges of Port Numbers

blocks.content: 4. Well Known Ports Worth Memorizing

You will run into a small handful of well known ports constantly, both in this course and in real engineering work. These are worth genuinely memorizing rather than looking up every time, the same way you already know that a web address usually starts with https.

{"headers":["Port","Service","What it is used for"],"rows":[["80","HTTP","Standard, unencrypted web traffic"],["443","HTTPS","Encrypted web traffic, the padlock in your browser"],["22","SSH","Secure remote login to another machine"],["21","FTP","File transfer between machines"],["25","SMTP","Sending email between mail servers"],["53","DNS","Translating domain names into IP addresses"]]}

blocks.title: DNS gets its own module later
blocks.content: Port 53 shows up constantly because DNS runs on it, but the full story of how DNS actually resolves a name into an address is big enough to deserve its own dedicated module later in this course. For now, just recognize port 53 as the DNS port.
5. How a Client Picks Its Own Port
blocks.text: 5. How a Client Picks Its Own Port

blocks.content: Here is a detail that trips people up the first time they think about it carefully. When your browser opens a connection to a web server, the server side is easy to explain, it sits listening on a well known port, 443 for HTTPS, patiently waiting for connections to arrive. But what port does your browser itself use?

Your browser does not use port 443, or any other well known port, on its own side of the connection. Instead, your own operating system hands it a random, temporary ephemeral port, something like 51422, pulled from that dynamic range you just saw in the table above. This happens automatically, every single time, without you ever noticing or configuring anything.

The reason this matters is purely about routing responses correctly. When the server sends its reply back, that reply needs to land on the exact browser tab or request that asked for it, not on any other program running on your machine at the same time. The ephemeral port is what makes that possible, it is the unique return address your own device stamped on the outgoing request.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436868214-306352069.png
blocks.alt: How a Client Picks Its Own Port

blocks.content: 6. Sockets: The Real Identifier of a Conversation
blocks.text: 6. Sockets: The Real Identifier of a Conversation

blocks.content: A socket is the pairing of an IP address and a port number together. On its own, a socket describes one endpoint of a conversation, this device, on this port. But a full network connection is not just one socket, it is a relationship between two of them.

A specific network connection is actually identified by the combination of four things at once: the source IP, the source port, the destination IP, and the destination port. This four part combination, often just called the socket pair, is exactly what lets a single server handle thousands of simultaneous connections from different clients without ever mixing them up.

It also explains something that looks impossible at first glance. The same client can open multiple connections to the very same server, on the very same destination port, at the very same time, and the server still keeps every one of them perfectly separate. It can do this because even though the destination IP and destination port are identical across all those connections, the source port on the client side is different for each one, and that difference is enough to tell them apart.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436868214-111551271.png
blocks.alt: Sockets: The Real Identifier of a Conversation

blocks.content: 7. A Worked Example

Picture a single web server sitting at IP address 93.184.216.34, listening on its well known port, 443. Three different clients decide to connect to it at roughly the same moment. Client A has IP 10.0.0.5 and gets handed ephemeral port 51001. Client B has a completely different IP, 10.0.0.9, and gets ephemeral port 51002. Client C, interestingly, shares the exact same IP as Client A, 10.0.0.5, perhaps a second browser tab on the same laptop, but it gets handed a different ephemeral port, 51003.

All three of these connections arrive at the server aimed at the identical destination, 93.184.216.34 on port 443. And yet the server never confuses them, because it is not tracking connections by destination alone. It is tracking each one by its full four part combination: source IP, source port, destination IP, destination port. Client A's traffic is 10.0.0.5:51001 talking to 93.184.216.34:443. Client C's traffic is 10.0.0.5:51003 talking to that same destination. Same source IP, different source port, and that alone is enough to keep them as two entirely separate conversations.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436868214-75710208.png
8. Why Ports Matter for Security

Ports are not just a routing mechanism inside one device, they are also one of the most basic tools in network security. Firewalls commonly work by simply blocking or allowing traffic based on port number. A firewall rule might say, allow anything coming in on port 443, block everything else, and that single rule already does a huge amount of protective work.

This is also why closing unused ports is such a standard, repeated piece of security advice. Every open port on a machine is a potential doorway, a program listening and willing to respond to whoever reaches it. A port with nothing legitimate listening on it, left open anyway, is pure unnecessary risk with no corresponding benefit.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436868214-179642574.png

blocks.title: A useful mental model
blocks.content: Think of every open port as an unlocked door on a building. Well known doors that need to stay unlocked, like the front entrance for HTTPS traffic on 443, stay open on purpose. Every other door that nobody actually needs should be locked, because an open door nobody is watching is exactly how intruders get in.
9. Common Mistakes

The single most common mistake is assuming that an IP address alone is enough to identify a specific network conversation. It is not, and this course has now built up the full reason why across two connected topics. An IP address identifies a device, nothing more. The moment a device is running more than one networked program at once, which is true of almost every real device almost all of the time, the IP address stops being specific enough on its own.

A closely related mistake is forgetting that a client's ephemeral port is just as real and just as necessary a part of a connection as the server's well known port. It is easy to mentally treat the server's port, 443 or 80, as the important one and wave away the client's random port as an unimportant implementation detail. But as the worked example above showed directly, that ephemeral port is doing genuine, load bearing work. Without it, a server could never tell two connections from the same client apart.
/engineering/library/cn/images/1785436868215-327790788.png
